name: serve
description: Serves local directories on loopback HTTP. When published with --pub <subdomain>, the directory is gated behind Cloudflare Access at <subdomain>.princess-pi.dev, admitting only the emails listed in that directory's .serve-acl. The allow-list is what isolates one preview from another — the login prompt is not, because Cloudflare authenticates once per account and shares that identity across every preview. The Cloudflare account and domain are currently hardcoded — this tool assumes you're running on Princess Pi's VPS with her Cloudflare credentials. Logs HTTP access to ~/.config/princess-pi-packages/serve/logs/. Available as the /serve command inside Pi Coding Agent, or as the standalone ./serve CLI script from any shell.

why.scenario: You're developing a site or web app and want a live-reloading local preview of your build output.
why.result: dist/ is served on an auto-assigned local port (8080) with live reload; the clickable URL is printed in the TUI widget. Pass --pub <name> to publish it as an Access-gated preview at <name>.princess-pi.dev.

why.scenario: You forget which directory to serve, or just want to see what's already running before starting more.
why.result: serve lists the servers running in this repo, then suggests an agent prompt to locate a servable dir (e.g. "find the servable build/output dir here and serve it"). Nothing is started — you name the dir explicitly.

why.scenario: You've got stale dev servers from a previous session and need to clean them all up.
why.result: Every active server across all worktrees is terminated immediately.

why.scenario: You want to check what directories are currently being served, on which ports, and at what URLs.
why.result: Every active server on this machine is listed with full paths, ports, types, and clickable URLs.

why.scenario: You want to take down a public preview URL but keep the local dev server running.
why.result: The Cloudflare ingress and Access app for the sub-domain are removed. The local server keeps running — republish anytime with --pub.

why.scenario: You want to serve only static files (no live-reload injection) — for example, testing production builds locally.
why.result: Directories are served as plain static files without code injection or file-watching overhead.

why.scenario: You want to deploy a site to production or serve traffic to the public internet.
why.result: The serve tool is a local development preview server only — not a production web server. Publish previews with `serve <dir> --pub <slug>` (Cloudflare Tunnel + Access); use Railway or another production deployment tool for public-facing services.

why.scenario: An agent or script needs to know what is being served without parsing a TUI table.
why.result: One JSON document, schema serve/list@1, one flat record per server (pid, port, dir, kind, subdomain, url, localUrl, title). The human table is free to change because this exists.

usage.desc: Serve the specified directories on local ports. With no dir, serve lists running servers and suggests how to find one (no default dirs — starts nothing).
Disable live reloading and serve pure static files without code injection or file watching.
Bypass the .env secret warning and serve the directory anyway. CLI only — Pi prompts interactively instead.

Publish the target dir as a gated preview at <subdomain>.princess-pi.dev, admitting only the emails in the directory's .serve-acl. Without --pub, serve runs local-loopback only. Note the gate authorizes per sub-domain but authenticates once per Cloudflare account: someone already signed in to another princess-pi.dev preview AND listed in this .serve-acl opens this one with no login prompt at all, while someone signed in but not listed here gets the login page and is sent no code. Since a first visit can therefore be silent, verify the gate with `curl -sI https://<subdomain>.princess-pi.dev/` (expect 302 to cloudflareaccess.com), never from a signed-in browser.

List every server serve started that is still running (full paths, ports, types, URLs). Servers serve did not start are not listed.
Kill servers by port, directory, or 'all'. Requires explicit targets - bare --kill is a no-op. Only kills servers serve started; server-like processes it did not start are reported and left running.

Machine-readable output for --list and --kill. Emits one JSON document (schema serve/list@1 or serve/kill@1): flat, one record per server, stable keys. Exit codes: 0 success (an empty result set is success), 1 operation failed, 2 usage error.
